lesson.title: -eur Discrimination Drills
lesson.subtitle: Convert -or/-er nouns to -eur and decide le vs la using the agent vs quality rule.

hook.title: Fast Sorting: Masculine Agents vs. Feminine Qualities
hook.content: Run the -eur bridge at full speed, separating masculine human agents (un docteur, un acteur, un directeur, un professeur) and masculine bonheur/honneur from feminine quality nouns (une couleur, une erreur).

footnotes.title: How un/une reveals the gender when l' hides it
footnotes.content: On vowel-initial l'acteur, l'honneur, and l'erreur, the definite article elides to l' — so testing with un/une (un acteur, un honneur, une erreur) makes the gender visible!

pattern.title: Convert -or → -eur, Then Check Agent (un) vs. Quality (une)
pattern.content: Use the Agent vs. Quality rule across mixed drills.
pattern.linguist_note: Agentive -eur (< -ātōrem) vs. abstract -eur (< -ōrem) converged phonetically while diverging in gender.
pattern.trap_note: Watch out for l'erreur vs. l'acteur: l'acteur is a person (un bon acteur), while l'erreur is a quality (une grande erreur)!

exercises.prompt: Sort these -eur nouns into un (masculine) vs. une (feminine):
exercises.target_answer: un docteur, un acteur, un honneur, une couleur, une erreur
exercises.meaning: a doctor (person), an actor (person), an honour (masculine exception), a color (quality), an error (quality)
exercises.explanation: un/une reveals the gender even when l' hides it.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence has the correct gender agreement?
options: C'est un bon acteur et un grand erreur
C'est une bonne acteur et un grand erreur
C'est un bon acteur et une grande erreur
exercises.target_answer: C'est un bon acteur et une grande erreur
exercises.meaning: He is a good actor (m.) and it's a big mistake (f.)
exercises.explanation: acteur is masculine (un bon acteur); erreur is feminine (une grande erreur).

exercises.prompt: Convert English 'the professor / teacher' to French (with article):

exercises.idea: the director and the professor are here
cues: and the professor are here → et le professeur sont ici
idea_parts: subjects → Le directeur et le professeur
exercises.target_answer: Le directeur et le professeur sont ici
exercises.meaning: The director and the professor are here
exercises.explanation: Both human agent nouns take le, and together they take plural sont.

diagnosis.cue: Two singular subjects joined by et take plural sont.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: C'est un grand honneur pour moi
exercises.target_answer: C'est un grand honneur pour moi
exercises.meaning: It is a great honour for me
exercises.explanation: honneur is masculine (un grand honneur) and starts with a mute H.
exercises.affirmation: You paired un grand with honneur and pour moi.

summary.outcome: Discriminate masculine and feminine -eur nouns at speed and pair them with accurate articles and adjectives.

use_example.german: C'est un grand honneur de voir le directeur.
use_example.english: It is a great honour to see the director.

summary.takeaway: Check un/une when l' hides the article: un acteur, un honneur, une erreur.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([9] vous & tu): see how -eur Discrimination Drills leads directly into vous & tu.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "The director and the professor are here" in French:
twist.target_answer: Le directeur et le professeur sont ici
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Le directeur et le professeur sont ici" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of -eur Discrimination Drills.

docteur.etymology_derivation: Latin doctor 'teacher'. -or/-er nouns convert to -eur and are usually masculine.

directeur.etymology_derivation: Latin directus 'straight-lined' — the one who keeps things straight.

professeur.etymology_derivation: Used for any school or university teacher.

honneur.etymology_derivation: honour/honneur — a Norman doublet hiding in the -eur family.

bonheur.etymology_derivation: bon 'good' + heur 'fortune' (Latin augurium 'omen' — English 'augury'). Happiness is luck, well met.

couleur.etymology_derivation: Latin color → couleur — feminine, the famous exception the -eur squad warns you about.

erreur.etymology_derivation: Like la couleur, l'erreur kept its Latin feminine gender from abstract qualities.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
